In addition to the variable aperture lens, the main camera aperture of the iPhone 18 Pro is also wider than previous generations. Apple has been promoting this, claiming it can produce a shallower depth of field for portraits and similar scenes.

However, the difference between the two is less than one aperture stop, and given the small sensor size, how much difference it actually makes in real shooting has always been doubtful, so I decided to test it myself...

Portraits, not Portrait mode

First, a distinction needs to be made: the optical shallow depth of field produced by the wide-aperture lens, and the artificial effect created by Portrait mode.

The latter uses computational photography combined with the LiDAR sensor to calculate the boundary between subject and background, then applies an artificial blur effect. This effect has improved significantly over the years, but that is not what this test is about. All background blur effects in the sample photos were achieved optically at the maximum aperture of f/1.48.

A simple test method

The maximum aperture of the iPhone 17 Pro is f/1.78, which is essentially indistinguishable from the second-largest f/1.8 aperture on the iPhone 18 Pro. This test takes advantage of the newly added manual control feature, shooting the same scene at f/1.8 and f/1.48 respectively, in order to compare the difference between the two.

However, there are three other optical factors that affect the degree of background blur:

  • Focal length of the lens
  • Distance between subject and background
  • Distance between subject and camera

To eliminate these variables, all photos were taken at the same focal length (i.e. the main lens, which is the only one equipped with a variable aperture), the same composition (i.e. the same background), and the same distance. Each aperture adjustment was separated by a few seconds, so the photos are not 100% identical, but I and the subject both remained still, ensuring that even if he turned his head during shooting, the shooting distance remained exactly the same in both photos.

With these conditions controlled, any difference in the degree of background blur is entirely due to the aperture.

Test photos

All test photos are portraits, i.e. head-and-shoulders close-ups, because this is exactly the type of shooting where a large aperture is most often used (which is also why Apple named its artificial effect Portrait mode).

In addition, by moving close enough to shoot a head-and-shoulders close-up, the expected visible background blur can be maximised. Compared with shooting from a greater distance, this provides a more effective basis for comparison, as the blur in the latter may be difficult to judge.

Finally, I have also included a few photos with background gradient effects, so you can observe how the focal point diminishes with distance.

Enough preamble, let's look at the results. Slide the slider all the way to the right to view the f/1.78 version, slide it all the way to the left for the f/1.48 version, and stop at any position to compare different parts of the image.

Conclusion

I think this photo best demonstrates the difference in effect, because the background covers a range of distances from a few feet to about a quarter of a mile:

Top comment by RC2257

Adding a variable aperture to such a small sensor cannot produce much bokeh — this is simply a limitation of the laws of physics.

As mentioned in the article, the digital background blur effect processed computationally on the iPhone has improved significantly over the years, and personally I prefer it to the bokeh produced by the 18 Pro's variable aperture.

The fountain is the closest element, at about 8 to 10 feet, and a clear difference can be seen here. The trees are about 30 feet away, with a smaller but still clearly discernible difference. The pagoda is about 70 feet away, and the difference is still fairly obvious but slightly reduced. With more distant elements — the bridge and buildings across the river — the difference is even more subtle: it is still clearly noticeable when deliberately looking for it, but I don't think most people would notice it on their own.

In terms of practical benefit, the following photo is a good demonstration. When using the f/1.78 aperture, the sense of separation between Chris and the background is somewhat marginal in some areas, such as the people dining in the restaurant in the upper right corner, and a section of building to the upper right of his head. After switching to the wider aperture, the sense of separation noticeably improved.

I had wondered how much difference this relatively small change could make, and now I have my answer. Whether the difference is significant is something you can judge for yourself from the sample photos; personally, I would describe it as fairly subtle, but actually larger than expected — in some cases already useful enough. Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments.

A wider aperture is not the only benefit of the new lens. In other situations, the manual control of the variable aperture also has its uses, which I will explore in a follow-up article.
